title: Burst handshake latency notes (scratchpad)
content:
Purpose / quick summary:
- Trying to capture reproducible steps for the intermittent spike we see when a tenant jumps from idle->high qps (burst handshake). Hypothesis: handshake cost = combination of cold KV-cache + CUDA context scheduling + runtime batching alignment.

Experiment setup (local dev cluster - dedicated pool replica):
- Model: llama-3-7B-fp16-qlora (compatible variant), sequence length cap 2048
- Hardware: 1xA100-80GB per replica (baseline), driver 535.x
- Runtime binary: inference-runtime:v1.18.3 (w/ opt-kv-cache-hotpatch applied)
- Client: custom loadgen (go) issuing Poisson arrivals, can ramp QPS instantly
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) for token generation, throughput (tokens/s), KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, kernel launch latencies (nvtx traces)

Test variants:
A) Cold start burst: start clients from 0 -> 300 qps at t=30s (instant ramp)
B) Warm caching: run steady 50 qps for 10m then jump to 300 qps
C) Staggered warmup: launch 3 waves: 50 qps -> +100 qps after 20s -> +150 qps after 40s
D) Prefetch pre-warm: send synthetic prefix requests to pre-populate KV cache just before ramp

Client command (simplified):
./loadgen --model-endpoint http://localhost:8080/generate --arrival poisson --qps 300 --ramp-instant --seq 512 --duration 120s --tokens-per-request 128

Observations (raw notes):
- Variant A shows a sharp p99 spike at t~32s lasting ~6s. p99 jumps from ~280ms to ~1.8s. p50 barely moves (80ms -> 120ms). Throughput dips by ~15% for the same window.
- KV cache hit rate drops to ~14% during spike window (expected) then recovers to 92% after ~9s.
- NVTX traces show repeated kernel initialization stalls (~2.5ms each) early in the burst; many small kernel launches serialized.
- GPU util climbs but shows increased SM idle time during spike — suggests stalls waiting on host-side scheduling / memcopies.
- Variant B (warm caching) reduces p99 spike magnitude and duration: p99 peak ~760ms, duration ~3s, KV hit rate stays >=72%.
- Variant C diffuses the spike: smaller transient p99 increases (~350–420ms) as each stair-step triggers smaller handshake overheads.
- Variant D (prefetch) yields the best result: p99 peak ~220ms (close to normal), KV hit rate >88% at ramp time.

Quick table (typical run numbers):
- Baseline (steady 50 qps): p50=75ms, p95=210ms, p99=280ms, tok/s=4200, kv_hit=94%
- Variant A peak: p50=120ms, p95=400ms, p99=1800ms, tok/s dip to 3600, kv_hit=14%
- Variant B peak: p50=95ms, p95=320ms, p99=760ms, tok/s dip to 3900, kv_hit=72%
- Variant D peak: p50=80ms, p95=220ms, p99=220ms, tok/s stable 4150, kv_hit=89%

Interpretation / hypotheses:
1) KV cache cold-miss dominates token-level latency early in burst; when many requests need to populate attention keys simultaneously, runtime stalls on serial writes/copybacks.
2) Kernel launch and small-kernel serialization add measurable milliseconds per request — visible in NVTX. When lots of new batch entries cause different kernel shapes, we pay per-shape overhead.
3) Host-side scheduling (workqueue + thread wakeups) shows contention spikes when many request threads reach enqueue at once.
4) Prefetching prefixes (or a short synthetic warmup traffic) amortizes KV fill and kernel warmup cost across time, drastically reducing p99 spikes.

Actionable notes / next experiments:
- Short-term mitigation: add optional pre-warm API (POST /v1/admin/prewarm) clients can call prior to burst windows. Implement server-side cheap prewarm that allocates KV entries asynchronously.
- Runtime change: batch KV population to avoid N small device transfers; aggregate key writes into chunked memcpy. Measure impact on 1k simultaneous new keys.
- Scheduler tweak: add jittered enqueue (randomized micro-delays) for newly accepted requests when arrival rate > threshold to spread wakeups across 50–200ms window.
- Add a "small-kernel cache" path: detect and reuse precompiled kernel launch configs for common (seq_len, batch) combos to reduce launch overhead.

Follow-ups to log / assign:
- Create a focused perf PR to implement async KV prewarm: GH issue GH:PR#4521 (linked). Assign to Maya.
- SRE: run canary in dedicated pool with 10 tenants hitting synthetic weekend traffic to validate prewarm behavior (JIRA INF-1283).
- Add microbench for kernel-launch cost: instrument per-kernel launch latencies (accumulate distribution) and log to metrics.

Misc small notes / gotchas:
- Observed one run where prefetch helped but p99 still had ~500ms tail — that run coincided with host memory pressure (OOM-killer churn) on the node. Need cross-check with node memory metrics.
- Driver version differences: 535.x vs 545.x showed small improvements for kernel launch times in a synthetic kernel test — but not enough to obviate prewarm.
- Ensure admin prewarm is opt-in and rate-limited to avoid a DOS vector.

Quick ASCII chart (p99 over time, Variant A):
 t=0s |----steady 280ms----|
 t=30s | spike: ======1800ms ====== | recovery->280ms at t=40s

Conclusions (short):
- Burst handshake is real and actionable. Cheap prewarm (client-driven or server async) provides large wins, plus scheduler jittering reduces observed tail. Prioritize prewarm + KV write batching as highest impact.

Notes for future: save synthetic prewarm payload used (prefix length 64 tokens, 4 synthetic reqs per concurrent slot) as an artifact; details in GH PR.

End of scratchpad.
